I woke up with the taste of metal in my mouth and the feeling that I had been somewhere else all night. The ceiling fan was making that little click it always makes on the third rotation, and I counted it without meaning to. One, two, three click. One, two, three click. The light through the blinds was thin and yellow, like someone had left a lamp on in another room and forgot to turn it off.

I have been thinking a lot about how much space there is inside a day. It seems small from the outside, 24 hours, a neat little box. From the inside it expands and contracts. Some mornings are a hallway. Some afternoons are a cathedral. This one feels like a kitchen at 7am. The kettle is whistling in another life.

I made coffee and didn't drink it. It sat there getting cold while I stared at the email I didn't want to answer. The subject line was neutral. That’s the worst kind. Neutral means they’ve rehearsed it. Neutral means they want something but don’t want to sound like they want it. I typed three different drafts and deleted them all. The cursor blinked. I think about how many hours of my life have been spent blinking at a cursor.

The apartment smells like laundry detergent and the faint sourness of the trash can I forgot to take out. The cat is asleep on the radiator, which is too hot for her but she doesn't care. She has perfected the art of being exactly where she is. I want that. I want to be able to decide that this spot, right here, is enough.

I keep returning to a memory from when I was nine and my grandfather taught me how to tie a tie. He had hands that were huge and knuckled and warm. He kept saying, "Don't rush the loop, kiddo, the loop is the whole thing." I never learned to tie a tie properly. I still buy clip-ons when I need one for a wedding. I think about that often, not because of ties, but because of loops. How we get stuck in them. How we think the knot is the point when it's actually the loop.

The news is on in the background. Someone is talking about numbers. Inflation, something, something. Numbers have become a weather report. You just check them and then go on with your day as if the rain won't get you wet. I wonder when that happened. When did we agree to treat the world like a forecast?

I went for a walk because I read that walking helps thinking. It doesn't. It helps forgetting. I walked past the same storefronts I pass every day. The florist has a new sign, handwritten, with a crooked heart. The bodega has a little chalkboard that says "Free samples on Fridays." It's Tuesday. I bought a mango even though I don't like mango. I wanted to make a choice that wasn't practical.

On the way back I saw a kid on a scooter with no helmet, both hands in the air, screaming something at the sky. His mother was jogging behind him, half laughing, half panicking. It felt like the most honest thing I'd seen all week. Pure, unedited joy with a safety net.

I am thinking about language. How we use words like "fine" to mean "I am not going to tell you." How we say "let's circle back" to mean "I never want to talk about this again." How we say "I’m good" and mean "I’m tired." If I could write a dictionary of the real meanings, it would be short and devastating.

There is a draft of a novel I started three years ago. It's 42,000 words of people not saying what they mean in a small town by the sea. I open it sometimes and I don't recognize the voice. It sounds younger, more certain. I wonder if I should delete it or keep it. I think I will keep it because it is proof that I once believed I could finish something.

My phone buzzes. It's a message from a friend I haven't spoken to in months. "Hey, random, but I was thinking about you." I stare at it. I want to respond with something clever and warm. I want to respond with "same." I end up typing "hey!! how are you?" and then deleting the exclamation marks. Punctuation is a moral choice.

I think about the people who will read this and wonder why I wrote it. That's okay. Writing has never been for an audience. It's for the part of me that needs to get the thoughts out of my head before they start breeding in the dark. There are so many thoughts. Some are small and bright like moths. Some are heavy and slow like stones.

The coffee is cold now. I pour it out. The sink gurgles. I wash the mug and dry it and put it back exactly where it belongs. Little rituals are the way we tell ourselves we are in control of something.

I have 1000 words. I have maybe 600. I don't know. Counting words feels like counting breaths. It distracts you from living them. So I will stop counting now. I will let this be what it is: a snapshot of a Tuesday morning in a kitchen that smells like detergent, with a cat on a radiator and a man who doesn't know how to tie a tie.

If you were here, I'd offer you the mango. It's probably too sweet. But it's bright and it smells like summer, which is strange because it's almost winter. I think that's what I want to hold onto. The strange brightness.

Okay.
